title: Why we\'re here: my story, and the story of Craveiral
vimeoName: Module 1 - Why we're here: my story, and the story of Craveiral

segments.text: Hello, I'm Pedro. And if you're watching this, it's because you're part of Graverell.
Maybe you started this week. Maybe you've been with us for years.
Either way, I want to start at the beginning. Because everything we do here, every decision we
make, every plate we serve, every bed we prepare, it all comes from one story. And I think you deserve
to hear it from me. Twenty years ago, I was a lawyer in Lisbon. I still am, actually. I never
stopped. But somewhere along the way, I realized that the life I was building was missing something.
I had the office, I had the career, I had everything that's supposed to add up to success.
And I kept dreaming about land, about farming, about getting my hands in the soil.
It sounds romantic when I say it now. Believe me, it didn't feel romantic when I was learning
how hard farming actually is. And then, one spring day, I found a field. A field of carnations
near São Teotônio, on the Costa Vicentina. In Portuguese, a field of carnations is a
Graverell. That's where the name comes from. It's not a marketing invention, it's literally what
the land was. I remember standing in that field and thinking, this is it. This is the place.
Nine hectares of wild Alentejo. Minutes from some of the most beautiful, unspoiled coastline in
Europe. No neighbors in sight. Sky so clear at night that guests still stopped me on the walkways to
point at the stars. That was 2010. We opened in 2018. Eight years. Let that sink in for a moment.
Eight years between the dream and the first guest. Eight years of licensing, of building,
of doubting, of running out of money and finding it again. Of convincing architects and engineers
and banks and, honestly, my own family. That a lawyer from Lisbon could build something real
in rural Odemira. Why am I telling you this? Not for sympathy. I'm telling you because I need you
to understand something fundamental. Graverell was not built to be a hotel. It was built to be
a relationship with a piece of land. The hotel is how we sustain that relationship. That order
matters. Land first, hotel second. When you understand that 100 small decisions we make
year suddenly make sense. Look at how the place is built. We have nine hectares. Do you know how
much of it is constructed? Four percent. Four. Everything else is farm, orchard, garden, pine
forest, open space. We could have built more houses. We could have made more money per square meter.
We chose not to because of the emptiness, the space, the silence at night that is the product.
Guests don't come here despite the fact that we built so little. They come because of it. The houses
themselves, 38 of them, are connected by raised wooden walkways. Have you ever wondered why we
built walkways instead of just paving paths? Because raised wood lets the land breeze underneath.
Water flows, plants grow, the soil stays alive. Even the way you walk to your house here
is a decision about respecting the land. Here's the phrase I want you to remember from this first
module. We say it in everything belong does. We do not own the land. We belong to it for a while.
Think about what that means for your work. If we own the land, our job would be to extract value
from it. Get the most out of it as fast as possible. But if we belong to it, then our
job is to leave it better than we found it. Better soil, better water, a stronger village,
a team that grows. Guests who live a little more connected to something real than when they arrived.
That's not a slogan for me. I gave up a quieter, easier life for this idea. And every person who
works at Creverell is whether you signed up for it or not. Part of that same idea now.
One more thing before we move on. People sometimes ask me, Pedro, was it worth it? Eight years?
All that risk? All that stress? And I always answer the same way. I've watched a child collect eggs
in the morning and run to show her parents like she'd found treasure. I've watched a couple get
married under our pine trees. I've watched people from the village find good, stable work five
minutes from home in a region where that is not a small thing. So yes, every single day it's worth it.
